question: What is buffered I/O and why is it important for performance?
title: Why Buffered I/O Matters
direct_answer: Buffered I/O reads or writes data in large chunks (typically 8KB) rather than byte by byte. This dramatically reduces system calls and disk access frequency. An unbuffered read of 100 bytes makes 100 system calls; a buffered read makes one.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not wrapping streams with buffered versions, causing performance issues
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that each read()/write() call translates to a native OS system call

sections.title: The Cost of Unbuffered I/O
sections.content: Every call to read() on an unbuffered FileInputStream eventually becomes a system call — a context switch between user space and kernel space. System calls are expensive. Reading a 1MB file byte by byte means 1,048,576 system calls. With BufferedInputStream (8KB default buffer), it takes 128 system calls. The difference is 1000x+ speedup.

sections.title: Buffered I/O Classes
content: BufferedInputStream: buffers byte stream reads (default 8192 bytes)
BufferedOutputStream: buffers byte stream writes, flushes when full or on flush()
BufferedReader: buffers character stream reads, provides readLine()
BufferedWriter: buffers character stream writes, provides newLine()
Default buffer size: 8192 bytes (8KB) — good for most cases
Custom size: new BufferedInputStream(stream, 65536) for 64KB buffer
Always wrap unbuffered streams: new BufferedReader(new FileReader(file))

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Buffered I/O is critical for performance. When you read from a FileInputStream directly, each read() call is a system call to the OS — expensive context switches. BufferedInputStream maintains an internal byte array, typically 8KB. When you call read(), it checks if data is in the buffer. If the buffer is empty, it reads 8KB from the OS in one system call, filling the buffer. Next 8000 reads come from memory — no system calls. This makes buffered reads orders of magnitude faster for small reads. Always wrap file streams with Buffered versions.

speakable_v2.hook: Unbuffered file I/O is like knocking on the OS door for every single byte — buffering batches those knocks.

beats.content: Every read() call on a raw FileInputStream is a system call — a round trip between your Java code and the operating system kernel. Those round trips are expensive. Reading a 1 MB file byte by byte triggers over a million system calls. Wrap it in BufferedInputStream and it takes 128 — one per 8 KB chunk.

beats.heading: The four buffered stream classes
items: BufferedInputStream — buffers bytes on the read side, default 8 KB
BufferedOutputStream — holds bytes in memory and flushes in chunks
BufferedReader — buffers characters and adds the readLine() method
BufferedWriter — buffers character writes and adds newLine()

beats.content: In our Java 17 config-reading app, wrapping FileInputStream with BufferedInputStream is a one-line change that can make file reads orders of magnitude faster. The rule of thumb: always buffer when reading from or writing to disk.

speakable_v2.familiarity_anchor: It's like loading groceries in bags instead of carrying one item at a time from the car.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app reading configuration files and writing logs

question: What is the difference between BufferedReader and BufferedInputStream?
title: BufferedReader vs BufferedInputStream
direct_answer: BufferedInputStream buffers raw bytes — use for binary data. BufferedReader buffers characters (text) and provides readLine(). BufferedReader handles character encoding; BufferedInputStream doesn't. For text files, always use BufferedReader. For binary files, use BufferedInputStream.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to choose the correct buffered stream for the data type
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using BufferedInputStream for text files and manually converting bytes to chars
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the composition pattern: BufferedReader(InputStreamReader(FileInputStream)) for explicit encoding

sections.title: Choosing the Right Buffered Stream
sections.content: The choice between BufferedReader and BufferedInputStream mirrors the choice between character streams and byte streams. If you're reading text and want lines, use BufferedReader. If you're reading binary data and want bytes, use BufferedInputStream. Don't use BufferedInputStream for text — you'll need to manually handle encoding.

sections.title: Comparison
content: BufferedInputStream: buffers bytes, read() returns int 0-255
BufferedReader: buffers chars, readLine() returns String
BufferedReader understands character encoding via underlying Reader
Best practice for text with explicit encoding: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(file), UTF_8))
Or in Java 11+: new BufferedReader(new FileReader(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
BufferedInputStream + DataInputStream: read primitives from binary data

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The difference mirrors byte stream versus character stream. BufferedInputStream buffers raw bytes — no awareness of characters or encoding. BufferedReader buffers characters and understands encoding through its underlying Reader. For text files, I use BufferedReader because I get the readLine() method and proper charset handling. For the most explicit and safe way: I construct BufferedReader wrapping InputStreamReader wrapping FileInputStream with explicit UTF-8 charset. This composition gives me buffering, character conversion, and explicit encoding in one chain.

speakable_v2.hook: BufferedReader and BufferedInputStream both buffer, but one speaks bytes and the other speaks text.

beats.content: BufferedReader knows about character encoding because it wraps a Reader, not an InputStream. That means it handles the byte-to-char conversion for you. BufferedInputStream doesn't know anything about encoding — it just moves bytes around.

For the safest text reading chain: BufferedReader wrapping InputStreamReader wrapping FileInputStream, with explicit UTF-8. That gives you buffering, encoding conversion, and explicit charset control all in one stack.

speakable_v2.familiarity_anchor: BufferedInputStream is a byte highway; BufferedReader is a text highway with a built-in translator.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app reading configuration files and writing logs

question: What does flush() do and when must you call it?
title: flush() in Java I/O
direct_answer: flush() forces any buffered data to be written to the underlying stream or destination. Call it on BufferedOutputStream or BufferedWriter when you need data written immediately, especially before closing or when sending partial data to a client.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of write buffering behavior and data loss risks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not flushing before closing, losing buffered data — though close() usually flushes
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that try-with-resources calls close() which calls flush() — but only if no exception occurs

sections.title: Why Flushing Matters
sections.content: Buffered output streams hold data in memory until the buffer fills or you flush. If your program crashes before the buffer fills, that data is lost. flush() forces immediate write to the underlying stream. close() calls flush() first, so properly closed streams don't lose data — but closing and flushing are separate concepts.

sections.title: When to Flush
content: Before closing: close() calls flush(), try-with-resources handles this
Partial writes: when sending incremental data (progress updates, log lines)
Network streams: flush to ensure data is sent immediately
PrintWriter auto-flush: new PrintWriter(writer, true) — flushes on println()
If close() throws exception: buffered data might not be flushed
System.out uses PrintStream which has autoFlush behavior

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: flush() forces any data held in the buffer to be written to the underlying destination. With buffered streams, write() puts data in memory — it might not reach the file or network immediately. You need flush() when you want data to reach the destination before the buffer fills. The common case where you don't need to call it explicitly: try-with-resources — when the block exits, close() is called, and close() calls flush() first. But if you're writing to a network socket and want the client to receive data incrementally, you must call flush() manually after each logical message.

speakable_v2.hook: flush() is the nudge that says stop holding onto those bytes and actually write them now.

beats.content: A buffered output stream holds your writes in memory until the buffer fills. That's great for performance, but it means data hasn't actually reached the file or network yet. flush() forces everything in the buffer out to the destination immediately.

beats.heading: When you must flush manually
items: Writing to a network socket incrementally — the client won't see data until you flush
Logging events one by one and you need each line visible right away
Handing off a stream to another process that reads it

beats.content: Try-with-resources calls close(), and close() calls flush() first — so a properly closed stream won't lose data. The danger is when an exception fires inside the try block before close() runs. That's the edge case where explicit flushing at checkpoints protects you.

speakable_v2.familiarity_anchor: Think of it like saving a document — the text sits in RAM until you hit Ctrl+S and it actually hits disk.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app reading configuration files and writing logs

question: How does BufferedReader's mark() and reset() work?
title: mark() and reset() in BufferedReader
direct_answer: mark(readAheadLimit) marks the current position. reset() returns to that position. This enables re-reading data — for example, to peek at the next token in a parser. Only works if the stream supports marking (BufferedReader and BufferedInputStream support it).

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of less common but important stream operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not checking markSupported() before calling mark()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a real use case like lookahead parsing

sections.title: mark() and reset() Use Case
sections.content: mark/reset lets you reread stream data. The readAheadLimit parameter tells the buffer how much data to keep in memory after the mark. If you read more than readAheadLimit bytes, the mark becomes invalid. Typical use case: parsing — peek at a token, decide how to interpret it, reset and re-read.

sections.title: Usage Pattern
content: markSupported(): check before using mark/reset (always call this first)
mark(readAheadLimit): set mark, buffer keeps readAheadLimit bytes
reset(): return to marked position
BufferedReader and BufferedInputStream support mark/reset
FileInputStream: does NOT support mark/reset by default
Use case: look-ahead parsing, detecting file format from header
PushbackInputStream: alternative for single-character lookahead

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: mark() and reset() allow you to go back in a stream. You call mark(N) to save the current position with a readAhead limit of N bytes. If you don't read more than N bytes forward, you can call reset() to return to the marked position. This is useful for lookahead parsing — peeking at what's coming to decide how to process it. Always call markSupported() first — not all streams support this. BufferedReader and BufferedInputStream do; raw FileInputStream doesn't. In practice, I rarely use mark/reset directly; parsers and format detectors are the main use cases.

speakable_v2.hook: mark and reset let you rewind a stream — useful for parsers that need to peek before deciding.

beats.content: Call mark(N) to bookmark your current position in the stream. N is the read-ahead limit — how many bytes the buffer must remember after the mark. Read forward, inspect the data, then call reset() to jump back to the bookmark and read it again.

beats.heading: Key rules
items: Always call markSupported() first — not all streams support it
BufferedReader and BufferedInputStream do support it; raw FileInputStream does not
If you read more than N bytes past the mark, the mark becomes invalid
PushbackInputStream is a simpler alternative when you only need to un-read one or two bytes

beats.content: In practice, mark and reset come up most in file format detection — read the first few bytes to identify the format, then reset and let the parser read from the beginning.

speakable_v2.familiarity_anchor: It's like a bookmark in a book — mark the page, read ahead, then flip back to the bookmark.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app reading configuration files and writing logs

question: When should you NOT use buffered I/O?
title: When Not to Buffer
direct_answer: Skip buffering when: the underlying stream is already buffered (database drivers, HTTP clients), you need byte-level control for network protocols, reading single bytes where latency matters more than throughput, or when working with memory-backed streams like ByteArrayInputStream.

interviewer_intent.testing: Nuanced understanding of when buffering adds vs subtracts value
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Double-buffering by wrapping an already-buffered stream
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that ByteArrayInputStream is already in memory so buffering adds no value

sections.title: Cases Where Buffering Is Counterproductive
sections.content: Buffering always adds a small overhead for allocating and managing the buffer. This overhead is negligible compared to disk I/O, but it's wasteful when the underlying source is already fast or already buffered.

sections.title: When Not to Buffer
content: ByteArrayInputStream: already in memory, buffering adds no value
StringReader: already backed by String in memory
Already-buffered underlying streams: avoid double-wrapping
Low-latency streaming: buffering adds latency to first byte delivery
Network protocols requiring byte-by-byte control
Test code: when working with small in-memory data for unit tests
In practice: the cost is negligible, err on the side of buffering for file I/O

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The main case where buffering adds no value is when the source is already in memory — like ByteArrayInputStream or StringReader. Wrapping them with Buffered versions just adds an extra layer without any performance benefit. Another case: some libraries provide their own internal buffering, and adding another Buffered layer on top creates double-buffering. That said, the overhead of an unused buffer is tiny, and it's better to have it than not for file I/O. I'd rather have a slight allocation overhead than accidentally read a 1MB file byte by byte. When in doubt, buffer.

speakable_v2.hook: Buffering is almost always good — but not when the data is already sitting in memory.

beats.content: Buffering solves the cost of repeated disk or network round trips. But ByteArrayInputStream and StringReader are already in heap memory — there's no disk to reach. Wrapping them with a Buffered class adds allocation overhead for zero performance gain.

beats.heading: Cases where you can skip the buffer
items: ByteArrayInputStream or StringReader — they're already in RAM
Streams from libraries that buffer internally — adding another layer just double-buffers
Low-latency protocols — buffering delays the first byte reaching the receiver

beats.content: That said, the cost of an unnecessary buffer is tiny. When in doubt for file I/O, buffer anyway. The worst outcome is a small allocation overhead; the worst outcome of forgetting to buffer is reading a large file one byte at a time.

speakable_v2.familiarity_anchor: Buffering solves a distance problem — if the data is already next to you, there's no distance to solve.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app reading configuration files and writing logs
